input.body:
The `claude-code-web-users-support` store held one `<email>.md` per person, so the only thing a person could carry into a session was prose. Each person now owns a **pack directory** in the store, poured into a session-only pack root that the engine loads like any other.

## The shape

`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory: `RULES.md`, an optional `pack.mjs`, `skills/`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start it is copied into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, and from there the existing loader does the rest: rules on the memory channel through the generated index, skills mounted, checks run.

**The engine gains two things.** A third pack root beside the canon and the repo's own local packs, active by presence rather than declaration (nothing about a person is the repository's to declare) and **opt-in per reader**, so a shelf conformance sweep, a vendoring pass or a catalog generator is answered as if the directory were not there. And a `session-prepare` phase on the existing step runner, running before anything reads the session's pack set, whose stdout is never session context.

**The index carries a literal line.** A generator running at converge time cannot discover a directory a session writes hours later, so the import is spelled out, and appears only where a declared pack ships a prepare step. The runner guarantees the file exists — empty when nobody's pack is there — so the import never dangles.

## Reaching the store

Local-first when this repo *is* the store, otherwise a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of the one directory. The GitHub tree API 403s behind the sandbox proxy and this repo's own guard records codeload as commonly denied where git against the same repository is not. Verified against the real store: the live pour from `missingbulb/Shepherd` found the owner's file and reported it.

## Compatibility

A person still on `<email>.md` is poured from it for one convergence window and told to convert; #2188 removes that tolerance. A member holding this pack beside an older engine pours late from the start step and injects the rules itself, so nobody's rules go missing in the window between the two delivery lanes — only their skills go unmounted.

## Folders touched

```
engine/pack_loader/    the third pack root and its opt-in, the prepare phase, the
                       index's literal line, the summary's exclusion of poured packs
engine/hooks/          the orchestrator runs the prepare phase first, with its stdout
                       redirected away from session context; session readers opt in
packs/claude-code-web-users-support/
                       the store now addresses a folder; pour.mjs does the work, the
                       prepare step calls it, the start step reports it, and the two
                       store checks judge directories and in-pack provenance
packs/claudinite-lifecycle/
                       the member-side index rule exempts the one import no checkout
                       can satisfy
engine-tests/, packs/*/test/
                       coverage for each of the above
```

## What was verified

- Whole suite green: 3798 tests, 0 failures.
- `check_the_world` exits 0, advisories only, all pre-existing but the empty provenance files this pack already had.
- The pour, both engine paths, the legacy file and the missing-pack case run end to end against a real git store.
- See-it-fail confirmed for the poured-pack reset, the index's literal line and the summary's exclusion.

Found along the way: importing the step runner for one constant ran its program and killed the importing process, and `path.relative` on two relative paths reaches for `process.cwd()` at import time, which faults in a process whose cwd was deleted. Both are fixed here.

Refs #2188

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-pack-prose

# Writing pack prose

Whether a candidate *qualifies* as a rule at all, and which mechanism carries it, is
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)'s call — settle it there before writing.

**Start from the foundation:** read the "Write each rule" section of
[authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md) first — its
principles (concrete enough to verify, motivation stated, what to do rather than what not to,
the right altitude, emphasis reserved) bind pack prose too. This skill is the pack-specific
layer on top of them, and doesn't restate them.

## The ration

Every rule in a `RULES.md` is paid for by every session in every repo that declares the pack,
forever, whether or not it ever applies — so prose is rationed, and the ration is small.

- **One sentence per rule, near 40 words**: the trigger, the directive, and a consequence
  clause only where the rule cannot be applied without it. A candidate that needs a paragraph
  to land has not been understood well enough to be a rule yet. (sentence-rule-near)
- **An extraction pass adds at most two rules.** If more candidates clear the bar, write the
  two strongest and drop the rest — they will recur if they were real. (extraction-pass-adds)
- **Split a rule that carries two situations.** Each situation is its own rule with its own
  trigger. (split-rule-carries)
- A `SKILL.md` loads only when its activity is under way, so it may carry procedure at length —
  but it is still rationed by the same test: every line must change what the reader does.
  Method, steps and decision points belong there; anything a session must know *without*
  loading it belongs in `RULES.md` or a check, and rationale belongs on the element's
  provenance file (below). (skill-md-loads)
- **Moving a rule out of `RULES.md` into a skill** — only where the skill's
  `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` covers *every* moment the rule is needed. A skill whose only
  trigger is its description is picked by the model, not the harness, so a rule that must fire at
  a moment no file edit predicts stays prose, however activity-shaped it reads. (moving-rule-out)
- **Starting a `SKILL.md`, or editing one that declares no body** — say under its frontmatter
  `metadata` what the body is: `body: workflow` for a procedure, whose steps and their gotchas
  change as one, or `body: guidelines` for rules behind a trigger, kept on the skill's one file
  until one has a history of its own. A skill that mixes the two declares the shape of its
  greater part. The harness ignores the key; the corpus's own maintenance reads it, and never
  infers it. (starting-skill-md)

## Shape a rule so it fires

- **Keying a rule to its trigger** — open with the act the reader is performing, not the state
  of the world the rule applies to. Nobody notices that "a value is unknown"; they notice they
  are writing an encoder. A rule keyed to a state never fires, because nothing brings the
  reader to it. (keying-rule-trigger)
- **Keying a rule the reader reaches while debugging** — name the symptom that sends them
  looking ("A fetch to a host you listed failing in-browser"), not the act that caused it. By
  the time the rule is wanted the act is over, and the symptom is what they can see.
  (keying-rule-reader)
- **Keying a rule that corrects a misconception** — name what the reader wants ("Wanting
  `import`/`export` in extension code"), not the wrong move they might make ("Reaching for a
  bundler"). Someone who doesn't yet know the move is wrong won't recognise themselves in it.
  (keying-rule-corrects)
- **Phrasing that trigger** — use the words the reader would use for the situation, and put
  them first and in bold, so the rule is findable by scanning the left margin alone.
  (phrasing-trigger)
- **Choosing the unit** — one block per situation, not one bullet per rule. A reader arrives
  holding a problem, so give them the whole decision in one place rather than a cross-reference
  to three neighbouring bullets. (choosing-unit)
- **Splitting a rule that only makes sense after the one above it** — don't. If the subject
  needs a "that" pointing back ("Writing that record"), it is a clause of the rule above, not a
  situation of its own. Split when a reader could arrive at the second rule without the first.
  (splitting-rule-only)
- **Separating the blocks** — one blank line between rules. The block is what a reader lands on,
  and an unbroken run of bullets makes them scan lines instead; the separation costs one token.
  (separating-blocks)
- **Ordering a file of many rules** — past roughly fifteen, group them under headings naming the
  surface each concerns, so a reader scans headings before subjects. A flat list that long makes
  every bold subject do the work one heading would. (ordering-file-many)
- **Grouping that separates two rules which qualify each other** — add an explicit pointer from
  the general rule to its exception, or the general one reads as unconditional. That pointer is
  the one sentence a rewrite may add that its source didn't have; name it as an addition when
  you report the change. (grouping-separates-rules)
- **Ordering the clauses** — the default first, then the `if you can't` fallback, then
  `consider` for an optional aid, then the `don't` that the earlier clauses make unnecessary.
  (ordering-clauses)
- **Choosing modality** — grade it per clause and claim no more than the rule needs. Keep
  `never` and `always` for the genuinely absolute and reach for `prefer`, `avoid` or `rather
  than` otherwise; escalating a `don't` into a `never` changes the rule rather than rewording
  it. (choosing-modality)
- **Naming a mechanism** — name the check, helper or skill that owns the mechanics, and stop.
  Its parameters, options and failure modes live with it, and restating them here is a copy
  that goes stale. The exception is a mechanism you are telling the reader to *run*, below.
  (naming-mechanism)
- **Telling the reader to *run* something** — ship the literal invocation in a fenced block, not
  the file's name. The reader is composing a call rather than looking a mechanism up, so a bare
  filename buys a probe every time — the `--help` that prints nothing, then the `cat`, then a
  hand-built command. (telling-reader-run)
- **Closing a block** — say what the other clauses make unnecessary ("don't also comment the
  duplication — the guard covers it"), so nobody adds belt-and-braces. (closing-block)
- **Keeping an exception** — an exception that changes what the reader would do is part of the
  rule; one that only reassures is padding. (keeping-exception)
- **Cutting a rule's prose** — drop rationale that only restates the rule, examples that
  re-express it, and mechanics another document owns. Keep the motivation itself: a consequence
  the reader needs in order to apply the rule under pressure earns its clause; rationale the
  reader doesn't need at act time goes on the element's provenance file (below).
  (cutting-rules-prose)
- **Auditing a file of rules that already exists** — take each rule and ask what a reader would
  get wrong without it. Fold the one whose subject points back at its neighbour; cut the one another
  pack already carries, the one a check now enforces (keeping only the half the check can't see),
  and the one whose mechanism has since been retired — a rule naming code that no longer exists
  teaches a world the reader won't find. (auditing-file-rules)
- **Rewriting an existing rule** — carry the source's own strength forward. A rewrite must not
  weaken a rule, and it must not strengthen one either. (rewriting-existing-rule)

## The provenance log - where a rule's rationale lives

A pack keeps one file per element under `provenance/`, beside its `RULES.md`: an append-only
log of the decisions behind the element, read by maintenance and review - the pass that asks
whether a rule still earns its place needs the reason it was written - and never by a session.
No rule sends its reader there, nothing loads it, and it never vendors: a member mounting a
canon pack receives the rules, not the reasoning behind them. The grammar, the kinds, the
fields and the tool are [changing-pack-elements](../changing-pack-elements/SKILL.md)'s; what
this skill adds is how a rule is written so the log can hold it.

- **Ending a rule** - every rule in a `RULES.md` ends with the bare marker naming its file -
  `… never a filesystem walk. (url-filter-host-operators)` - and nothing else: don't name the
  folder, don't link it, don't ask the reader to follow anything. The marker is the element's
  id: two to four hyphenated words for the guideline rather than its wording, chosen once and
  never renamed, so a rewording never touches it and a member's override can name it. Two
  rules whose history is one may share a marker. A guidelines skill's bullets are the skill's
  file's and carry none, until one's history diverges and it takes a marker and a file of its
  own; a workflow skill's steps carry none, the skill being the element. (ending-rule)
- **Adding a rule** - write the brief rule and end it with its marker; create its file with a
  `born` entry through `provenance.mjs append` (`mark` creates the file where none exists),
  and put the reason there, never in the rule. A consequence the reader needs under pressure
  earns its clause; rationale the reader doesn't need at act time is the entry's. Write the
  entry so a future review can **reaffirm the rule from it** - `Retire when` is what would
  have to be true for the rule to go. (adding-rule)
  - A **workaround** explains the issue with not using it, with the evidence (the failing run,
    the error, the measured cost).
  - A **technology guideline** cites the original documentation it derives from.
  - An **owner decision** carries the language of the request that set it - in a member's
    local pack; a canon file carries the paraphrase, never the quote.
- **Rewording, moving, splitting or converting a rule** - the entry is owed in the same
  change, and the forced skill names its kind. (rewording-moving-splitting)
- **A check's rationale** - on the check's own file, named by its id (`cer/version-bumped` →
  `cer-version-bumped.md`); nothing is added to the check. (checks-rationale)
- **Removing a rule or check** - its file stays and gains a `retired` entry as its last, in
  the same change. (removing-rule-check)

The `provenance-integrity` check holds the mechanism together - every carrier names a live
file, every file parses - and `provenance-change-recorded` holds the change: a carrier that
changed lands with its entry. A pack not yet on the convention is put there by
`provenance.mjs mark`, and its history filled by the
[backfilling-provenance](../backfilling-provenance/SKILL.md) skill; nothing here is done rule by
rule.

## Evidence

The commit and its PR remain the archive - the story of the incident, quoted exchanges and
session ids live there and in the capture, never in the rule and never in a canon's log. What
an entry takes from them is only the **reaffirmable core**: `Source` and `Reason`, the minimum
a future review needs to re-test the rule, and `Retire when`, the test it is reaffirmed
against. Keep a measurement inline in the rule only where the number *is* the argument - a cost
the reader wouldn't believe stated qualitatively.

4	// One resolver, because three readers need the same answer and must never disagree:
5	// the session-prepare step that pours a person's pack into the session, the session-start
6	// step that reports what it found, and the conformance rules that say whether this pack is
7	// configured and whether a store this repo holds is addressable at all.
8	//
9	// THE SHAPE, on this pack's own entry in `.claudinite-settings.json`:
10	//
11	//   { "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
12	//
13	// `repo` is required - the store is a repository, because what a person carries belongs
14	// to them rather than to any one project, and a repo is the smallest thing that can hold
15	// it for a whole fleet without living inside any member of it. `path` is where the people
16	// sit in that repo and defaults to `preferences`.
17	//
18	// ONE DIRECTORY PER PERSON, AND IT IS A PACK. `<path>/<email>/` is an ordinary pack
19	// directory - `RULES.md`, `pack.mjs`, `skills/`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`,
20	// `provenance/` - poured into the session's own pack root and loaded by the same engine
21	// that loads the canon and the repo's own packs. A person who wants a rule enforced, a
22	// skill mounted or a requirement installed writes it the way every other pack is written,
23	// rather than in whatever a bespoke preferences format happened to support.
24	//
25	// ONE PACK PER PERSON, not a shelf: the rules index addresses the poured prose by a fixed
26	// literal path (engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs states why), and a person is a person
27	// rather than a corpus.
28	//
29	// Dependency-free and pure: the caller supplies the parsed config, so this module
30	// touches neither disk nor network and is testable standalone.
31	
32	export const DEFAULT_PATH = 'preferences';
33	
34	// `{ repo, path }` when the config names a usable store, else null. Null covers both
35	// "nothing declared" and "declared but unusable" deliberately: every caller's next
36	// move is the same either way, and the difference is reported once, by the rule that
37	// exists to report it.
38	export function resolveStore(config) {
39	  if (config === null || typeof config !== 'object' || Array.isArray(config)) return null;
40	  if (typeof config.repo !== 'string' || !/^[^/\s]+\/[^/\s]+$/.test(config.repo)) return null;
41	  if (config.path !== undefined && (typeof config.path !== 'string' || config.path.includes('..') || config.path.startsWith('/'))) return null;

43	  return { repo: config.repo, path: path || DEFAULT_PATH };

46	// Where one person's pack sits inside the store, as a repo-relative directory path. An
47	// address only - whether it is read from a working tree or fetched over the network is
48	// the caller's business.
49	export function folderFor(store, email) {
50	  return `${store.path}/${email}`;
51	}

53	// The pre-folder address: one Markdown file per person, holding prose and nothing else.
54	// Read for one convergence window so a person whose file has not been converted yet is
55	// not silently left without their rules; the advisory the prepare step raises is what
56	// gets it converted, and #REMOVAL takes both back out.
57	// @legacy-tolerance advisory:person-asking-record retire:#2188

69	// segment and a URL component, so an implausible one is refused rather than
70	// traversed with: `../../x` as an "email" would address an arbitrary directory.

72	  && /^[^\s/\\]+@[^\s/\\]+$/.test(email)

1	# claude-code-web-users-support pack
2	
3	What a project can offer the people working on it **from the web** — a Claude Code web session runs
4	for a signed-in person in a managed container, and a terminal session does neither, so this is where
5	the capabilities that depend on knowing *who* is here — or on the managed container they get —
6	live. Today that is two: the pack each person brings with them, poured into the session by
7	[`session-prepare.mjs`](session-prepare.mjs) from a configured store repo; and
8	[`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh), the generic body a project pastes
9	into its web environment's **Setup script** field so the image carries the toolchains the base image
10	doesn't ship. The script's content is the same for every project — it just runs every active pack's
11	declared `env` install through the engine's `env-requirements.mjs`, so it never changes as
12	requirements do (bootstrap.md Part 9 walks the setup). Nobody has to go looking for that body:
13	the pack's `adoptionHandover` step has the filing session quote it inline, so the issue asking
14	for the paste carries the block to copy. The file stays the canonical copy because core may not
15	name a pack — `bootstrap.md` and the engine's env check reach it by its unique filename.
16	
17	Declared, and seeded by `--init`. The pack holds an **address**, not the content: `config.repo` (and
18	an optional `config.path`, default `preferences`) name the store that holds one `<email>/` directory
19	per person.
20	
21	## The pack a person brings
22	
23	`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory - `RULES.md`, optional `pack.mjs`,
24	`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start
25	[`pour.mjs`](pour.mjs) copies it into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, the engine's session
26	pack root, where the same loader that reads the canon and the repo's own packs picks it up: its
27	rules ride the memory channel through the rules index, its skills are mounted, its checks run, its
28	`env` is installed. So a person is not limited to stating preferences - anything a pack can carry,
29	they can carry.
30	
31	It is poured only into an **attended** session: a routine fired under a person's account carries
32	their identity but not their presence, and the harness's attended flag is what the step reads. Every
33	miss - unattended, no identity, no configured store, no directory, a clone that fails - is one
34	plain-text note from [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs) and the session proceeds on default
35	interaction behaviour. Reading is local-first: when this repo *is* the store, the working copy wins
36	over the default branch, so an edit in progress is what the session sees. Otherwise the store is
37	reached by a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of that one directory.
38	
39	Being the store also constrains the tree: the directory name is the whole address, so each one is
40	one person's exact identity, which [`worldRules/store-file-names.mjs`](worldRules/store-file-names.mjs)
41	explains and audits.
42	
43	**The store is as trusted as this repository.** A person's pack is executable code - checks and
44	hooks that run inside every session it is poured into - so write access to a person's directory is
45	the power to run code in their sessions. Protect the store's `<path>/` with branch protection or
46	per-directory code owners.
47	
48	What a person's pack carries is **personal, not project conventions**: conventions belong to the
49	packs that own each subject and load as prose, while these travel with a person across every project
50	they work in, and two people on one project can want different things.
51	
52	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
53	
54	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
55	|---|---|---|---|
56	| Changing a person's rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
57	| A person's first personal pack | high | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`preferences-store-file-names`) |
58	| A person wanting more than rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
59	| A web session's missing toolchain | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
60	
61	## Checks
62	
63	All three are advisory: a personal pack is a nice-to-have, and nothing here may block a session.
64	
65	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
66	|---|---|---|---|
67	| `preferences-store-configured` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
68	| `preferences-store-file-names` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
69	| `preferences-provenance` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

1	import { readdirSync, existsSync } from 'node:fs';
2	import { join } from 'node:path';
3	
4	// WHAT A PACK'S DIRECTORY ALREADY SAYS, AND WHAT SILENCE MEANS. Most of the
5	// manifest's fields had, in every pack ever written, exactly one correct value —
6	// either the one the pack's own tree already gave, or the one that means "this
7	// pack does not do that". The id repeated the directory name; `badge` and `prose`
8	// named the two files beside the manifest; `skills`, `worldRules` and `workRules`
9	// listed subdirectory and module contents the loader can read for itself; and
10	// `detect: null, marker: null` said, in two lines per pack, that a pack carries no
11	// fingerprint. A field with exactly one correct value is not a declaration; it is
12	// a line every author copies and every reviewer skips.
13	//
14	// So this is the manifest's DEFAULT LAYER and `pack.mjs` states only what neither
15	// the tree nor silence can: the pack's version, its routing guidance, an actual
16	// fingerprint, its adoption questions. Discovery was already structural — a
17	// directory with a pack.mjs is a pack — and this is the same principle one level
18	// in.
19	//
20	// OVERRIDE, NOT REPLACEMENT. A manifest field still wins where it is declared, so
21	// a pack that genuinely differs says so: `prose: null` beside a RULES.md that is
22	// documentation rather than injected rules, a `skills` subset that withholds a
23	// directory from mounting. The merge is a plain spread — the conventions are the
24	// base object, the manifest the override — which means an explicitly declared
25	// `null` overrides too, and only an ABSENT field falls through to the tree.
26	//
27	// The one filesystem read in the manifest layer. `pack-schema.mjs` stays pure (the
28	// caller hands it the facts); this module is the caller's other half, so the two
29	// together are "read the tree, then judge the result".
30	
31	// The conventional filenames. Named here rather than spelled at each use so the
32	// convention is one edit, and so a reader looking for "where does RULES.md become
33	// prose" lands on the answer.
34	export const PROSE_FILE = 'RULES.md';
35	export const BADGE_FILE = 'badge.svg';
36	export const SKILLS_DIR = 'skills';
37	// The pack's decision log, one file per element beside the carriers
38	// (engine/checks/helpers/provenance.mjs owns the grammar). Named here with the other
39	// conventional names because two readers with nothing else in common agree on it:
40	// the vendor set drops the folder from every mount, and the checks judge it.
41	export const PROVENANCE_DIR = 'provenance';
42	
43	// A rule's scope is its PLACEMENT — which was always true, and used to mean the
44	// manifest list it sat in. It now means the directory it sits in, one rung out:
45	// `<pack>/worldRules/*.mjs` audit repo state, `<pack>/workRules/*.mjs` judge the
46	// change and the session. The names are the manifest field names they replace, so
47	// a reader who knows one knows the other, and `RULE_SCOPES` in pack-schema.mjs is
48	// still the single vocabulary both sides read.
49	export const RULE_DIRS = ['worldRules', 'workRules'];
50	
51	// A pack with no fingerprint says nothing at all. `null` is what every reader
52	// already means by "not fingerprinted" — the declaration is authoritative and the
53	// drift check stands down in both directions — so silence resolves to it rather
54	// than to `undefined`, and no reader has to handle a third state.
55	const UNFINGERPRINTED = { detect: null, marker: null };
56	
57	// The skill directory names a pack bundles: every subdirectory of `<pack>/skills/`.
58	// A SKILL.md is NOT required here — a directory may carry only a skill's checks —
59	// because this answers "what does the pack bundle", and it is `bundledSkillSources`
60	// (the mount) that asks the narrower "what can a session load". Absent or
61	// unreadable skills/ reads as none; the registry's own scan reports the unreadable
62	// case, where it can name the fault.
63	export function bundledSkillDirs(packDir) {
64	  const root = join(packDir, SKILLS_DIR);
65	  if (!existsSync(root)) return [];
66	  try {
67	    return readdirSync(root, { withFileTypes: true }).filter((d) => d.isDirectory()).map((d) => d.name).sort();
68	  } catch {
69	    return [];
70	  }
71	}
72	
73	// The rule modules in one scope's directory, in filename order: every `*.mjs`
74	// that is not a test, each default-exporting one rule. A module that fails to
75	// import, or exports no rule, is reported by the caller — this returns the
76	// { file, module } pairs and judges nothing, so the loader can name the file in
77	// its diagnostic.
78	//
79	// FILENAME ORDER, not an author's chosen order. A manifest list carried one, and
80	// nothing downstream depended on it: the runners sort findings themselves and a
81	// pack's rules never see each other. Sorting here makes the set deterministic
82	// across filesystems, which the list could not guarantee either.
83	export function ruleModuleFiles(packDir, scope) {
84	  const root = join(packDir, scope);
85	  if (!existsSync(root)) return [];
86	  try {
87	    return readdirSync(root, { withFileTypes: true })
88	      .filter((d) => d.isFile() && d.name.endsWith('.mjs') && !d.name.endsWith('.test.mjs'))
89	      .map((d) => d.name)
90	      .sort()
91	      .map((name) => join(root, name));
92	  } catch {
93	    return [];
94	  }
95	}
96	
97	// What the pack directory named `name` says about itself. `badge` and `prose` are
98	// omitted rather than nulled when their file is absent, so a pack that declares
99	// neither and carries neither ends up with the fields simply not present — which
100	// is what every reader already treats as "no badge" / "no prose".
101	export function packConventions(packDir, name) {
102	  const conventions = { id: name, skills: bundledSkillDirs(packDir), ...UNFINGERPRINTED };
103	  if (existsSync(join(packDir, PROSE_FILE))) conventions.prose = PROSE_FILE;
104	  if (existsSync(join(packDir, BADGE_FILE))) conventions.badge = BADGE_FILE;
105	  return conventions;
106	}
107	
108	// The manifest as the loader consumes it: the tree's answer, overridden by
109	// whatever the manifest actually declares. A non-object export is handed back
110	// untouched — the spec is what reports that, and inventing an object here would
111	// turn a broken pack into a plausible one.
112	export function applyPackConventions(mod, packDir, name) {
113	  if (mod === null || typeof mod !== 'object' || Array.isArray(mod)) return mod;
114	  return { ...packConventions(packDir, name), ...mod };
115	}
116	
117	// THE SESSION-PREPARE STEP a pack may ship: the phase that runs before anything reads the
118	// session's pack set, for a pack that has to PUT SOMETHING THERE for those readers to find
119	// (run-pack-session-start.mjs states the phase). Discovered structurally, like every other
120	// convention here - a pack contributes one by shipping the file.
121	//
122	// The name and the predicate live in this module, not with the runner that spawns it,
123	// because the rules index also has to ask the question (a repo whose packs pour nothing
124	// imports nothing poured) and the runner is a CLI entry point: importing it to borrow one
125	// constant runs it.
126	export const PREPARE_FILE = 'session-prepare.mjs';
127	
128	// A pack the registry loaded always carries `dir`; one a caller built by hand may not, and
129	// the answer for a pack with no directory is that it ships nothing.
130	export const shipsPrepareStep = (pack) => typeof pack?.dir === 'string' && existsSync(join(pack.dir, PREPARE_FILE));

input.body:
The `claude-code-web-users-support` store held one `<email>.md` per person, so the only thing a person could carry into a session was prose. Each person now owns a **pack directory** in the store, poured into a session-only pack root that the engine loads like any other.

## The shape

`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory: `RULES.md`, an optional `pack.mjs`, `skills/`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start it is copied into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, and from there the existing loader does the rest: rules on the memory channel through the generated index, skills mounted, checks run.

**The engine gains two things.** A third pack root beside the canon and the repo's own local packs, active by presence rather than declaration (nothing about a person is the repository's to declare) and **opt-in per reader**, so a shelf conformance sweep, a vendoring pass or a catalog generator is answered as if the directory were not there. And a `session-prepare` phase on the existing step runner, running before anything reads the session's pack set, whose stdout is redirected away from session context.

**The index carries a literal line.** A generator running at converge time cannot discover a directory a session writes hours later, so the import is spelled out, and appears only where a declared pack ships a prepare step. The runner guarantees the file exists, empty when nobody's pack is there, so the import never dangles.

## Reaching the store

Local-first when this repo *is* the store, otherwise a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of the one directory. The GitHub tree API 403s behind the sandbox proxy and this repo's own guard records codeload as commonly denied where git against the same repository is not. Verified against the real store: the live pour from `missingbulb/Shepherd` found the owner's file and reported it.

## Compatibility

A person still on `<email>.md` is poured from it for one convergence window and told to convert; #2188 removes that tolerance.

A member holding this pack beside an older engine pours late from the start step and injects the rules itself, so nobody's rules go missing in the window between the two delivery lanes; only their skills go unmounted.

`consumer-safe-change` asked which of the three answers this takes for the two exports it removes. **Re-export shims**, not a migration record and not a fixture: `fileFor` now aliases `legacyFileFor` and `provenanceDirOf` stays where it was, both deprecated and both retired by #2188 with the tolerance they belong to. A record would move the fleet for a rename nothing here requires, and a fixture would only prove the canon's own packs still converge.

The two engine exports this pack newly reads come through a namespace import with a capability guard, for the same reason the late pour exists: the lanes deliver separately, and a named import of an export a member's engine lacks is a link-time error that faults the whole pack.

**Two rules were deliberately reworded**, which `rules-append-only` reports as removals: `person-asking-change` and `person-asking-record` keep their ids and their strength, and now name a directory where they named a file. Both carry the entry on their provenance file.

## Folders touched

```
engine/pack_loader/    the third pack root and its opt-in, the prepare phase, the
                       index's literal line, the summary's exclusion of poured packs
engine/hooks/          the orchestrator runs the prepare phase first with its stdout
                       kept out of session context; the session readers opt in
packs/claude-code-web-users-support/
                       the store addresses a folder now; pour.mjs does the work, the
                       prepare step calls it, the start step reports it, and the two
                       store checks judge directories and in-pack provenance
packs/claudinite-lifecycle/
                       the member-side index rule exempts the one import no checkout
                       can satisfy
engine-tests/, packs/*/test/
                       coverage for each of the above
```

## What was verified

- Whole suite green: 3798 tests, 0 failures.
- `check_the_world` and `check_the_work` both exit 0, with no blocking findings.
- The pour, both engine paths, the legacy file and the missing-pack case run end to end against a real git store.
- See-it-fail confirmed for the poured-pack reset, the index's literal line and the summary's exclusion.

Found along the way, and fixed here: importing the step runner for one constant ran its program and killed the importing process, and `path.relative` on two relative paths reaches for `process.cwd()` at import time, which faults in a process whose cwd was deleted.

Refs #2188

content: Explain the change.

content.text:
## The problem it solves

The `claude-code-web-users-support` pack knows who is in front of a web session, because the harness puts the person's identity in the environment. It used that to read one Markdown file per person out of a store repository and print it into the session. That file could only ever carry prose.

What people actually want to carry is more than prose. A skill they reach for. A check that catches the mistake they keep making. A toolchain their own tools need installed. Every one of those already has a carrier in this system, the pack, with an engine that mounts, runs and reports it. So the change stops inventing a delivery path per capability and makes a person's content an actual pack.

## How it works

Each person now owns a directory in the store, `<path>/<email>/`, and that directory is an ordinary pack: [`RULES.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/packs/claude-code-web-users-support/README.md), an optional manifest, `skills/`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. A person who only wants rules writes one file and nothing else, because [`pour.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/packs/claude-code-web-users-support/pour.mjs) writes the manifest for them.

At session start that directory is copied into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`. The engine's [pack registry](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/engine/pack_loader/pack-registry.mjs) now treats that path as a third pack root beside the canon and the repository's own local packs. From there nothing is special-cased. The existing loader mounts the skills, runs the checks, reads the `env`, and the rules ride the memory channel through the generated index rather than hook stdout, which is the channel #807 measured being silently truncated.

Two properties of that root are deliberate and worth stating. It is **active by presence**, not by declaration, because nothing about a person is the repository's to declare and a declaration naming one person would sit in a file every other person reads. And it is **opt-in per reader**: only the session-time readers ask for it, so a shelf conformance sweep or a catalog generator is answered as if the directory were not there. Without that second property, one person's pack reads as a pack the repository carries, which is how the first version of this broke the badge check, the README index and 78 vendoring rehearsals at once.

The ordering forced one engine addition. The skill mount, the self-test and the index all read the session's pack set before the existing step runner fires, so a pack arriving at that point is one nothing sees. There is now a `session-prepare` phase on the same runner, running first, whose stdout the orchestrator redirects away from session context. A prepare step is doing something, not saying something.

The index line is a literal. A generator running when a repository converges cannot discover a directory a session writes hours later on another machine, so the import is spelled out, and it appears only where a declared pack ships a prepare step. That is what makes adopting the pack the thing that adds the line. The runner guarantees the file exists, empty when nobody's pack is there, so the import never dangles.

## What it costs and what it protects

Reaching the store is a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse clone of the one directory, local-first when the repository being worked in *is* the store. I tried the tree API first and it returns 403 behind the sandbox proxy, and this repository's own guard already records codeload as commonly denied where git against the same repository is not.

Two fallbacks keep anyone from losing rules during the transition. A person still on the old single file is poured from it and told to convert, which [#2188](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/2188) removes. A member holding the new pack beside an older engine pours late from the start step and injects the rules itself, so the only thing lost in that window is the skill mount.

The honest cost is trust. A person's pack is executable code that runs inside the hooks of every session it is poured into, so write access to someone's directory in the store is the power to run code in their sessions. That is in the pack's README as a instruction to protect the store with branch protection or per-directory code owners, because no cap in the pour substitutes for it.

Two defects surfaced while building it. Importing the step runner to borrow one constant ran its program and exited the importing process, which made a whole test file pass by never running. And `path.relative` on two relative paths reaches for the working directory at import time, which throws in a process whose directory has been deleted. Both are fixed on the branch.

> ✅ All done: [PR #2189](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2189) carries the change, 3798 tests pass, both sweeps exit clean.

1	# claude-code-web-users-support pack
2	
3	What a project can offer the people working on it **from the web** — a Claude Code web session runs
4	for a signed-in person in a managed container, and a terminal session does neither, so this is where
5	the capabilities that depend on knowing *who* is here — or on the managed container they get —
6	live. Today that is two: the pack each person brings with them, poured into the session by
7	[`session-prepare.mjs`](session-prepare.mjs) from a configured store repo; and
8	[`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh), the generic body a project pastes
9	into its web environment's **Setup script** field so the image carries the toolchains the base image
10	doesn't ship. The script's content is the same for every project — it just runs every active pack's
11	declared `env` install through the engine's `env-requirements.mjs`, so it never changes as
12	requirements do (bootstrap.md Part 9 walks the setup). Nobody has to go looking for that body:
13	the pack's `adoptionHandover` step has the filing session quote it inline, so the issue asking
14	for the paste carries the block to copy. The file stays the canonical copy because core may not
15	name a pack — `bootstrap.md` and the engine's env check reach it by its unique filename.
16	
17	Declared, and seeded by `--init`. The pack holds an **address**, not the content: `config.repo` (and
18	an optional `config.path`, default `preferences`) name the store that holds one `<email>/` directory
19	per person.
20	
21	## The pack a person brings
22	
23	`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory - `RULES.md`, optional `pack.mjs`,
24	`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start
25	[`pour.mjs`](pour.mjs) copies it into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, the engine's session
26	pack root, where the same loader that reads the canon and the repo's own packs picks it up: its
27	rules ride the memory channel through the rules index, its skills are mounted, its checks run, its
28	`env` is installed. So a person is not limited to stating preferences - anything a pack can carry,
29	they can carry.
30	
31	It is poured only into an **attended** session: a routine fired under a person's account carries
32	their identity but not their presence, and the harness's attended flag is what the step reads. Every
33	miss - unattended, no identity, no configured store, no directory, a clone that fails - is one
34	plain-text note from [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs) and the session proceeds on default
35	interaction behaviour. Reading is local-first: when this repo *is* the store, the working copy wins
36	over the default branch, so an edit in progress is what the session sees. Otherwise the store is
37	reached by a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of that one directory.
38	
39	Being the store also constrains the tree: the directory name is the whole address, so each one is
40	one person's exact identity, which [`worldRules/store-file-names.mjs`](worldRules/store-file-names.mjs)
41	explains and audits.
42	
43	**The store is as trusted as this repository.** A person's pack is executable code - checks and
44	hooks that run inside every session it is poured into - so write access to a person's directory is
45	the power to run code in their sessions. Protect the store's `<path>/` with branch protection or
46	per-directory code owners.
47	
48	What a person's pack carries is **personal, not project conventions**: conventions belong to the
49	packs that own each subject and load as prose, while these travel with a person across every project
50	they work in, and two people on one project can want different things.
51	
52	## Rules (`RULES.md`)
53	
54	| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
55	|---|---|---|---|
56	| Changing a person's rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
57	| A person's first personal pack | high | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`preferences-store-file-names`) |
58	| A person wanting more than rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
59	| A web session's missing toolchain | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |
60	
61	## Checks
62	
63	All three are advisory: a personal pack is a nice-to-have, and nothing here may block a session.
64	
65	| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
66	|---|---|---|---|
67	| `preferences-store-configured` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
68	| `preferences-store-file-names` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
69	| `preferences-provenance` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- backfilling-provenance: Filling a pack's empty provenance files from its history - one pack per pull request, each entry derived from the adding commit, its pull request and the version log before the rule is re-read, and the README trimmed to use in the same change. Use when a pack under packs/ or .claudinite/local/packs/ carries empty provenance files, or when asked to backfill or write a pack's provenance.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- changing-pack-elements: What a change to a pack's element owes - the entry on its provenance file, which kind, and how to append it - and what a pack's README carries. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md, skills, checks, tasks, manifest, README or provenance folder, in a repo's local pack or on a canon's shelf.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the basics pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- learning-a-technology: Teach a repo a new technology for a job of its own — research it against the vendor's live documentation, capture what is portable as a technology skill with declared checks, and wire the project's use of it as a task in its structural local pack. Use when asked to make a repo do something with a technology nobody there has used yet (host it on X, send through Y, publish to Z), or to "research how to do this correctly" and "create a skill" for it.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- revalidating-rules: Re-probe the pack rules whose truth lives outside the repository — harness tool contracts, token reach, whether an MCP tool exists, a platform's behaviour — and correct the ones that have gone stale. Use when a revalidation sweep runs over a corpus of packs, or when asked whether a rule's environmental claim still holds.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- searching-for-a-tool: Finding a harness tool by name — the select form for a deferred tool, and what an empty search means. Use before any ToolSearch, and when a search finds nothing.
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, get the owner's approval of the plan itself — a line per step, the dependency graph, each link's automerge policy — before filing any of its issues, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written - RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon - brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, the marker that names a rule's provenance file. Loaded for any edit of a pack's RULES.md or SKILL.md, and when landing a lesson as prose.
- writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

# claude-code-web-users-support — working from Claude Code on the web

- **A person asking to change one of their personal rules** - edit the pack that travels with
  them, `<path>/<email>/` in the store repo this pack names, never here and never in the canon,
  and append the entry on the rule's provenance file inside that pack, the person the actor; a
  project convention in disguise belongs in the pack owning its subject, and a rule triggering a
  command owns only the trigger phrase. (person-asking-change)

- **A person asking to record their personal rules with nothing there yet** - create
  `<path>/<email>/RULES.md` in that store repo, the directory named for their exact identity,

Loaded Claudinite from repo missingbulb/Claudinite: 8 packs, 15.4k context tokens, 32 guards, 94 code checks, 17 auto-trigger skills, 19 regular skills, 550 personal pack tokens.

Worth noting first: the session-start line above now reads 8 steps and 550 personal pack tokens, which is this change running on itself. Your rules reached this session through the pour.

## What the pour is

[`pour.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/packs/claude-code-web-users-support/pour.mjs) exports one function, `pour({ root, config, env })`. It copies the pack belonging to the person in front of the session out of the store and into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, then returns a receipt saying what happened. It is synchronous, it never throws, and it always leaves a loadable pack behind, even an empty one.

Two callers share it, which is why it is a module rather than a step. [`session-prepare.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/packs/claude-code-web-users-support/session-prepare.mjs) calls it in the phase before anything reads the session's pack set, which is where it belongs. [`session-start.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/bold-planck-1nx6ru/packs/claude-code-web-users-support/session-start.mjs) calls it only when it finds no receipt, meaning that phase does not exist in this member's engine yet.

## The sequence

It gates first, and each gate is a receipt outcome rather than an error. No configured store, an unattended session, no identity in the environment, an identity that is not usable as a directory name. Attendedness matters because a routine fired under your account carries your identity but not your presence, and a rule like "ask every decision through a popup" misdirects a run nobody is watching.

Then it finds a source. If this checkout already holds `<path>/<email>/`, that is the source, because in the store repository itself the working copy is what you are editing and a clone would serve the default branch instead. Otherwise it clones: `--depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse`, then a sparse-checkout set to that one directory plus the retired `<email>.md` beside it. Either way what comes back is a directory in a working tree, so one reader covers both cases and a test points the clone at a local path.

Then it filters and budgets. Only `.md`, `.mjs` and `.json`, at most 60 files and 512KB. Past either limit it stops with a receipt rather than a partial pack.

Then it empties the destination before writing. That matters more than it looks: an earlier session in the same container may have poured a different person's pack, or an older version of yours, and content nobody in this session chose must not survive into it. That is the one behaviour I mutated deliberately to watch the test go red.

Then it writes, path-checking each file against the destination it claims to sit in, counting words in the Markdown for the token facet, and synthesising a manifest if the person's directory carries none. Their own `pack.mjs` is poured untouched when they have one, and it must set neither `id` nor `version`: the engine takes a poured pack's id from its directory, and that directory belongs to the session rather than to the store.

## The receipt

`.pour.json` beside the poured `RULES.md`, holding the outcome, where it came from, the files, the word count and whether the legacy file was the source. It exists because the two halves of this are split: the prepare phase does the work and says nothing, and the start step reads the receipt and writes the one note you see. An absent receipt is its own signal, distinct from a pour that found nothing, and it is what triggers the late-pour fallback.

That fallback is the only place the pour's output reaches you as prose. On an engine with the prepare phase, your rules arrive through the rules index on the memory channel and the start step stays quiet about them.

> ✅ All done: the pour is a single fail-soft function, two callers, one receipt, on [PR #2189](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/2189).

# claude-code-web-users-support pack

What a project can offer the people working on it **from the web** — a Claude Code web session runs
for a signed-in person in a managed container, and a terminal session does neither, so this is where
the capabilities that depend on knowing *who* is here — or on the managed container they get —
live. Today that is two: the pack each person brings with them, poured into the session by
[`session-prepare.mjs`](session-prepare.mjs) from a configured store repo; and
[`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh), the generic body a project pastes
into its web environment's **Setup script** field so the image carries the toolchains the base image
doesn't ship. The script's content is the same for every project — it just runs every active pack's
declared `env` install through the engine's `env-requirements.mjs`, so it never changes as
requirements do (bootstrap.md Part 9 walks the setup). Nobody has to go looking for that body:
the pack's `adoptionHandover` step has the filing session quote it inline, so the issue asking
for the paste carries the block to copy. The file stays the canonical copy because core may not
name a pack — `bootstrap.md` and the engine's env check reach it by its unique filename.

Declared, and seeded by `--init`. The pack holds an **address**, not the content: `config.repo` (and
an optional `config.path`, default `preferences`) name the store that holds one `<email>/` directory
per person.

## The pack a person brings

`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory - `RULES.md`, optional `pack.mjs`,
`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start
[`pour.mjs`](pour.mjs) copies it into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, the engine's session
pack root, where the same loader that reads the canon and the repo's own packs picks it up: its
rules ride the memory channel through the rules index, its skills are mounted, its checks run, its
`env` is installed. So a person is not limited to stating preferences - anything a pack can carry,
they can carry.

It is poured only into an **attended** session: a routine fired under a person's account carries
their identity but not their presence, and the harness's attended flag is what the step reads. Every
miss - unattended, no identity, no configured store, no directory, a clone that fails - is one
plain-text note from [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs) and the session proceeds on default
interaction behaviour. Reading is local-first: when this repo *is* the store, the working copy wins
over the default branch, so an edit in progress is what the session sees. Otherwise the store is
reached by a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of that one directory.

Being the store also constrains the tree: the directory name is the whole address, so each one is
one person's exact identity, which [`worldRules/store-file-names.mjs`](worldRules/store-file-names.mjs)
explains and audits.

**The store is as trusted as this repository.** A person's pack is executable code - checks and
hooks that run inside every session it is poured into - so write access to a person's directory is
the power to run code in their sessions. Protect the store's `<path>/` with branch protection or
per-directory code owners.

What a person's pack carries is **personal, not project conventions**: conventions belong to the
packs that own each subject and load as prose, while these travel with a person across every project
they work in, and two people on one project can want different things.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Changing a person's rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| A person's first personal pack | high | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`preferences-store-file-names`) |
| A person wanting more than rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| A web session's missing toolchain | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |

## Checks

All three are advisory: a personal pack is a nice-to-have, and nothing here may block a session.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `preferences-store-configured` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
| `preferences-store-file-names` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `preferences-provenance` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

# claude-code-web-users-support pack

What a project can offer the people working on it **from the web** — a Claude Code web session runs
for a signed-in person in a managed container, and a terminal session does neither, so this is where
the capabilities that depend on knowing *who* is here — or on the managed container they get —
live. Today that is two: the pack each person brings with them, copied into the repo by
[`session-prepare.mjs`](session-prepare.mjs) from a configured store repo; and
[`environment-setup-command.sh`](environment-setup-command.sh), the generic body a project pastes
into its web environment's **Setup script** field so the image carries the toolchains the base image
doesn't ship. The script's content is the same for every project — it just runs every active pack's
declared `env` install through the engine's `env-requirements.mjs`, so it never changes as
requirements do (bootstrap.md Part 9 walks the setup). Nobody has to go looking for that body:
the pack's `adoptionHandover` step has the filing session quote it inline, so the issue asking
for the paste carries the block to copy. The file stays the canonical copy because core may not
name a pack — `bootstrap.md` and the engine's env check reach it by its unique filename.

Declared, and seeded by `--init`. The pack holds an **address**, not the content: `config.repo` (and
an optional `config.path`, default `preferences`) name the store that holds one `<email>/` directory
per person.

## The pack a person brings

`<path>/<email>/` in the store is an ordinary pack directory - `RULES.md`, optional `pack.mjs`,
`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `worldRules/`, `declared-checks.json`, `provenance/`. At session start
[`pour.mjs`](pour.mjs) copies it into `.claudinite/temp/packs/current_user/`, the engine's session
pack root, where the same loader that reads the canon and the repo's own packs picks it up: its
rules ride the memory channel through the rules index, its skills are mounted, its checks run, its
`env` is installed. So a person is not limited to stating preferences - anything a pack can carry,
they can carry.

It is poured only into an **attended** session: a routine fired under a person's account carries
their identity but not their presence, and the harness's attended flag is what the step reads. Every
miss - unattended, no identity, no configured store, no directory, a clone that fails - is one
plain-text note from [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs) and the session proceeds on default
interaction behaviour. Reading is local-first: when this repo *is* the store, the working copy wins
over the default branch, so an edit in progress is what the session sees. Otherwise the store is
reached by a shallow, blob-filtered, sparse `git clone` of that one directory.

Being the store also constrains the tree: the directory name is the whole address, so each one is
one person's exact identity, which [`worldRules/store-file-names.mjs`](worldRules/store-file-names.mjs)
explains and audits.

**The store is as trusted as this repository.** A person's pack is executable code - checks and
hooks that run inside every session it is poured into - so write access to a person's directory is
the power to run code in their sessions. Protect the store's `<path>/` with branch protection or
per-directory code owners.

What a person's pack carries is **personal, not project conventions**: conventions belong to the
packs that own each subject and load as prose, while these travel with a person across every project
they work in, and two people on one project can want different things.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Changing a person's rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| A person's first personal pack | high | correctness | prose: <50 words + check (`preferences-store-file-names`) |
| A person wanting more than rules | medium | complexity | prose: <100 words |
| A web session's missing toolchain | medium | complexity | prose: <50 words |

## Checks

All three are advisory: a personal pack is a nice-to-have, and nothing here may block a session.

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `preferences-store-configured` | medium | complexity | check: advisory |
| `preferences-store-file-names` | high | correctness | check: advisory |
| `preferences-provenance` | low | complexity | check: advisory |

# This fleet's per-user preferences

One file per person — `<email>.md` — holding that person's **personal interaction
preferences**: tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are
surfaced, and the phrases they use to trigger defined commands.

These are **not** project conventions. Project conventions are shared canon and live in
[Claudinite's `packs/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs), which every
fleet mounts. Personal preferences are the concern of **this fleet's users**, which is why they
live here, in the fleet's own repo, and not in the canon: the canon is the wrong host for one
owner's preferences and the wrong authority on where they belong.

## How a session finds them

Each member of the fleet declares the `claude-code-web-users-support` pack in its own
`.claudinite-checks.json`, and names this repo as the store:

```json
{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "missingbulb/Shepherd" } }
```

That pack's session-start step reads `preferences/<the session user's email>.md` from it —
locally when the session is *in this repo* (the working copy is the truth here), over HTTPS
otherwise. Every miss is fail-soft: one note in the session context, and the session proceeds
on default interaction behavior.

The declaration is written into each member by this repo's `fleet-pack-seeds` sweep, from the
`packSeeds` list on this repo's own sheepdog config — which is why no consuming repo has to know
this repo's name by hand. Neither Claudinite's engine nor the sheepdog pack knows what any of
this is *for*: the engine runs the pack's step because the pack ships one, and the sweep seeds
the declaration because this repo's config names it.

## Adding or editing preferences

Add a file named for the person's email address, or edit theirs. One distilled preference per
bullet, in the imperative — a preference is a rule the assistant can act on, not a description
of a mood. Nothing here is secret, but nothing here needs to be shared either: it is the
fleet's own repo, and it stays that way.

# This fleet's per-user packs

One directory per person — `<email>/` — holding the **pack that travels with them**: how they
want to be worked with (tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the phrases they use to
trigger defined commands), and anything else a Claudinite pack can carry.

These are **not** project conventions. Project conventions are shared canon and live in
[Claudinite's `packs/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs), which every
fleet mounts. A person's own pack is the concern of **this fleet's users**, which is why it
lives here, in the fleet's own repo, and not in the canon: the canon is the wrong host for one
person's rules and the wrong authority on where they belong.

## What a person's directory holds

`<email>/` is an ordinary pack directory. The only file most people need is `RULES.md`. A
person who wants more can add any of:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `RULES.md` | the rules, loaded into every session they open on a member repo |
| `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | a skill of their own, mounted like any pack's |
| `worldRules/`, `workRules/`, `declared-checks.json` | checks of their own |
| `provenance/` | the decision log behind each rule, one file per rule |
| `pack.mjs` | a manifest, only where one is needed; it sets neither `id` nor `version` |

Because it is copied into every session on every member repo, it may hold nothing that belongs
to one project. A project convention goes in the pack that owns its subject.

## How a session finds it

Each member of the fleet declares the `claude-code-web-users-support` pack in its own
`.claudinite-settings.json`, and names this repo as the store:

```json
{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "missingbulb/Shepherd" } }
```

That pack copies `preferences/<the session user's email>/` into the member's session pack root
before anything reads it — from the working copy when the session is *in this repo*, by a
shallow sparse clone otherwise. From there the member's own engine loads it like any other
pack. Every miss is fail-soft: one note in the session context, and the session proceeds on
default interaction behavior.

The declaration is written into each member by this repo's `fleet-pack-seeds` sweep, from the
`packSeeds` list on this repo's own sheepdog config — which is why no consuming repo has to know
this repo's name by hand. Neither Claudinite's engine nor the sheepdog pack knows what any of
this is *for*: the engine runs the pack's step because the pack ships one, and the sweep seeds
the declaration because this repo's config names it.

## Adding or editing a person's pack

Create `<their exact email>/RULES.md`, or edit theirs. The directory name is the whole address,
case included, so any other name is silently never read. One distilled rule per bullet, in the
imperative — a rule is something the assistant can act on, not a description of a mood.

**Write access here is the power to run code in someone's sessions**: a pack's checks and
skills execute inside every session it is copied into. Treat a change under someone else's
directory as you would a change to their repo.

Nothing here is secret, but nothing here needs to be shared either: it is the fleet's own repo,
and it stays that way.

the declaration because this repo's config names it.

bullet, in the imperative — a preference is a rule the assistant can act on, not a description
